evaluation.positioning_hook: After a police killing ignites a zoo break-in, a grieving young woman and a ragtag crew get trapped inside a collapsing animal park where every enclosure becomes a death trap.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and built for trailer moments: a zoo, a riot, a tiger, a polar bear, and a final reveal that reframes the whole mission. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant crowd because the script is hard-edged, violent, and politically charged, but the genre engine is very sellable.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening pages: a police shooting, a viral backlash, and a revenge-driven zoo infiltration. The script keeps the central engine clear even as it escalates into a survival gauntlet.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: James has a strong contradiction: she is both emotionally wounded and operationally capable, and the supporting crew gives the movie multiple pressure points. The character work is strongest when grief, guilt, and identity collide in the gondola and sanctuary sequences, though some supporting roles are more functional than deeply singular.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldness comes from fusing social unrest, animal-escape spectacle, and a manipulation twist into one contained feature engine. The Dallas Zoo setting is not just backdrop; it becomes a story machine with distinct enclosures, rules, and escalating hazards.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Once the break-in begins, the script keeps stacking reversals: the tiger awakening, the polar bear, the mandrill attack, the gator crossing, and the final identity reveal. The momentum is strong because each set piece changes the survival math rather than repeating the same threat.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh because it is both immediately understandable and structurally unusual: a protest-fueled zoo heist that becomes a trapped-in-the-wild survival thriller. The late reveal that the guide is a trafficker weaponizing grief gives the premise a sharper, more cynical aftertaste.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The zoo is richly mapped with tunnels, exhibits, transport carts, veterinary rooms, and the tram system, and those spaces generate action rather than just scenery. The social texture around the riot, the staff hierarchy, and the animal-handling protocols gives the world a lived-in specificity.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is distinct: street-level anger collides with creature-feature spectacle and then folds into a bleak conspiracy thriller. The script knows when to be raw, when to be funny, and when to go full nightmare.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are deeper layers around grief, racial identity, manipulation, and the commodification of outrage, and the interrogation-room frame helps that land. The final twist suggests more beneath the surface, though the movie is still primarily driven by immediate survival stakes.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: James, Brett, Madyline, Terrell, and Chidi create a workable ensemble where loyalties keep shifting under pressure. The best relationship material comes from James/Brett, James/Madyline, and James/Terrell, though the movie still clearly belongs to James.

lead_characters.name: James McKenzie
lead_characters.demographics: Mixed-race woman, early 20s, Black/white, Dallas-based, grief-stricken and working-class.
lead_characters.hook: Dre’s cousin and the emotional center of the film, James is a young woman whose anger is real, whose guilt is corrosive, and whose sense of self is split between communities, loyalties, and versions of the truth. She starts as a grief-driven organizer and ends as someone forced to confront how easily righteous pain can be weaponized against her.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country or Letitia Wright in The Silent Twins: a role that demands physical command, emotional fracture, and a final moral reckoning. It gives an actor the chance to carry action, grief, and identity conflict in the same performance.

lead_characters.name: Terrell
lead_characters.demographics: Black man, early-to-mid 20s, Dallas local, armed, volatile, street-smart.
lead_characters.hook: Terrell is the movie’s volatility engine: funny, defensive, loyal in flashes, and increasingly dangerous as the night goes on. He reads like the friend who can turn a plan into a disaster and still believe he’s the only one thinking clearly.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Daniel Kaluuya in Widows or Lakeith Stanfield in Uncut Gems room to pivot between charm and threat. It offers a sharp, scene-stealing descent with real comic bite before the violence hardens him.

lead_characters.name: Chidi
lead_characters.demographics: Nigerian man, late 20s to 40s, zoo staffer, physically compromised by injury later in the film.
lead_characters.hook: Presented as a nervous, helpful zoo employee, Chidi is the film’s most consequential disguise: calm, competent, and quietly manipulative beneath the surface. The role plays as gentle support until the reveal turns him into the story’s hidden operator.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-reveal performance territory that made actors memorable in The Usual Suspects or Gone Girl: controlled, understated, then recontextualized. It gives an actor the chance to play two movies in one without telegraphing the turn.

lead_characters.name: Brett
lead_characters.demographics: White man, early 20s, James’s boyfriend, emotionally earnest, physically vulnerable.
lead_characters.hook: Brett is the well-meaning outsider who wants to help but never fully understands the stakes until it is too late. His love for James is sincere, but his presence also exposes the racial and emotional fault lines inside the group.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting territory in the vein of Ben Hardy in Bohemian Rhapsody or Jack O’Connell in Starred Up: a role that starts as support and becomes a gut-punch. The injury and sacrifice give the actor a real emotional payoff.

lead_characters.name: Madyline
lead_characters.demographics: White woman, early 20s, Brett’s friend or partner, anxious, conflicted, emotionally exposed.
lead_characters.hook: Madyline is the conscience in the room until she becomes another casualty of the night’s emotional and physical chaos. Her insecurity, jealousy, and fear make her feel human rather than functional, which is why her turn lands hard.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do escalating vulnerability the way Jessie Buckley did in Wild Rose or Kaitlyn Dever did in Short Term 12. It offers a strong emotional arc and a brutal survival sequence.

lead_characters.name: Corbett
lead_characters.demographics: White man, 40s, DART officer, Southern, armed, hardened.
lead_characters.hook: Corbett is the professional face of the zoo’s security apparatus: calm, capable, and lethal when the night goes sideways. He functions as a grounded authority figure until the chaos makes him just another predator in the system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid character-actor material in the lane of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Shea Whigham in any number of pressure-cooker thrillers. It gives an actor authority, menace, and a clean physical presence.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Miranda Sands
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 40s, lead veterinarian, professional, stressed, compassionate.
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Sands is the humane professional trying to keep order while the zoo’s systems fail around her. She adds a grounded, procedural layer to the chaos and gives the animal side of the story emotional credibility.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play competence under pressure, similar to Rebecca Ferguson in Doctor Sleep or Emily Blunt in Sicario. It’s a contained but memorable authority role.

lead_characters.name: Zoo Director
lead_characters.hook: The Zoo Director is the bureaucrat in panic mode, more concerned with liability and optics than ethics. He’s a useful pressure valve for the institutional side of the story and a clean target for the film’s contempt.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a classic pressure-cooker supporting part in the vein of Jeffrey Wright in a smaller authority role or John Turturro in a thriller ensemble. It gives an actor sharp, nervous energy and a few memorable beats.

lead_characters.name: Frey
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s to 30s, security tech, bored, underprepared.
lead_characters.hook: Frey is the night-shift weak link: distracted, casual, and tragically outmatched by what’s coming. He’s there to show how thin the zoo’s defenses really are.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but effective panic-role, the kind that lets an actor make a strong impression fast. It’s a good showcase for escalating fear and helplessness.

lead_characters.name: Abasi Ekwueme
lead_characters.demographics: Nigerian man, 30s to 40s, former anti-poaching officer turned trafficker, physically capable, manipulative.
lead_characters.hook: The man James knows as Chidi is actually Abasi, and the reveal recasts him as the film’s hidden architect: a trafficker who weaponizes grief, identity, and the language of justice. He is the movie’s most dangerous intelligence, because he doesn’t just survive the chaos — he authors it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-reveal villain role that can redefine an actor’s profile, like Walton Goggins in Justified or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom. It offers secrecy, menace, and a final-act payoff that changes the whole movie.

lead_characters.name: Real Chidi Obasanjo
lead_characters.demographics: Nigerian man, adult, zoo employee, off-screen or minimally seen in the frame story.
lead_characters.hook: The real Chidi exists as the film’s buried truth: the man whose identity was stolen to make the con work. He matters less as a presence than as the key that unlocks the ending.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a brief but important reveal role, the kind that can land like a gut punch if cast with precision. It gives an actor a single, high-impact turn in the final movement.

technical.vfx_details: Animal augmentation, safety removals, crowd enhancement, and some environmental chaos; the tiger, polar bear, mandrill, hippo, and escape beats will require a mix of practical, VFX, and compositing support.
technical.sfx_needs: Animal attack choreography, breakaway glass, blood effects, vehicle movement, rooftop crossing, and controlled chaos in enclosed spaces.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best suited to streaming-first or specialty theatrical with a strong genre marketing push.

budget.note: The zoo footprint, night exteriors, animal attack sequences, tram work, and multiple enclosed set pieces will push this above a simple contained thriller, but it remains scopeable without tentpole spend.

casting.note: James needs a lead who can carry grief, action, and identity conflict, while Chidi/Abasi requires a precise late-reveal performance that can play benign before turning predatory.

development.note: The final reveal recontextualizes the entire mission, so the script’s emotional contract depends on the audience accepting that manipulation without losing sympathy for James.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre fans who want a high-concept survival thriller with social heat, especially viewers who respond to elevated creature features and morally messy protagonists.
audience_target.demographics: Adults 18-44, slightly male-skewing but with real female-lead appeal; strongest with urban, streaming-native, and genre-literate audiences.

budget_tier.note: A contemporary zoo setting with multiple animal set pieces, night exteriors, stunts, and VFX-driven creature work places it in mid-budget feature territory.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where social urgency, contained spectacle, and a strong female lead can travel together. The zoo setting gives buyers a clean marketing image while the twist and racial politics give it conversation value.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The ending teases a larger conspiracy, but there is no clear franchise or spinoff vector with enough independent character depth to justify extension.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The zoo is a story machine.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the movie a built-in escalation engine that can justify a mid-budget spend because every enclosure, tunnel, and transport route can become a new set piece. Buyers can immediately see the trailer, the poster, and the production value on the page.
strengths.evidence: The script moves from African exhibit to tunnels to polar bear enclosure to tram to veterinary station to reptile pavilion to hippo lagoon, each space changing the threat profile.

strengths.dimension_or_area: James is a real lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The script offers a female lead with grief, rage, guilt, and physical agency, which is exactly the kind of part that can attract an actor looking to level up in genre. That makes the project more castable than a standard creature feature.
strengths.evidence: James drives the break-in, makes the key decisions, carries the emotional fallout, and ends in interrogation with the truth still unresolved.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The premise has immediate commercial clarity.
strengths.what_it_means: A zoo riot survival thriller is easy to pitch in one sentence and easy to market with animals, chaos, and a contained location. That clarity helps both buyers and audiences understand the movie fast.
strengths.evidence: The opening police shooting, viral outrage, and zoo infiltration set the engine in motion before the first major turn.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The twist re-frames the whole night.
strengths.what_it_means: The Chidi/Abasi reveal turns the movie from a straightforward revenge mission into a manipulation thriller, which adds replay value and post-screening conversation. That kind of structural sting is valuable for streamers and genre buyers.
strengths.evidence: The interrogation-room sequence reveals the guide was actually Abasi, and that the real Chidi was elsewhere the whole time.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The set pieces keep changing shape.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie avoids the flatness that can sink contained thrillers because each major sequence introduces a new animal, new terrain, and new survival logic. That makes the script feel bigger than its footprint.
strengths.evidence: Tiger attack, polar bear encounter, mandrill assault, gator crossing, and final cart chase all play differently.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, marketable elevated survival thriller with a strong female lead and a zoo setting that naturally generates trailer-ready set pieces. It has the kind of contained-but-spectacular production profile that can attract streamer genre teams or specialty theatrical buyers without needing franchise baggage.

items.area: The final reveal reassigns the whole movie.
items.detail: The Chidi/Abasi twist is smart, but it also asks the audience to retroactively accept that the emotional center of the mission was built on a con. That is a high-wire move in a feature, because the ending has to preserve James’s emotional journey while exposing how thoroughly she was manipulated.

items.area: The zoo footprint drives the budget up.
items.detail: The script uses a lot of distinct spaces — loading bay, tunnels, gift shop, rooftop, polar bear enclosure, reptile pavilion, hippo lagoon, tram — and each one wants its own production design and night coverage. That is still manageable, but it is not a cheap contained thriller.

items.area: The animal set pieces need careful safety translation.
items.detail: Tiger, polar bear, mandrill, hippo, black mamba, and alligator beats all appear in the same feature, which means the movie lives or dies on how convincingly those threats are staged. The script is clear about the danger, but the production has to solve a lot of creature work without the seams showing.

He moves from comic volatility to armed threat to outright betrayal, and the script lets him go very dark. That gives the movie bite, but it also means the ensemble’s emotional balance depends on the audience staying engaged with a character who becomes increasingly hard to root for.

items.area: The political anger is potent but polarizing.
items.detail: The opening police shooting and the viral outrage frame the movie in a very specific social conversation, and the ending’s media montage pushes that even harder. That gives the film urgency, but it also narrows the buyer conversation to platforms and distributors comfortable with overtly charged material.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction point is the late identity reveal, which is clever but structurally risky because it recontextualizes the emotional engine after the audience has already invested. On the production side, the zoo scale and multi-animal action are the main cost and execution conversations, even though the concept itself is very sellable.
